14091.content:
Design against negative consequences anticipates ways software could cause disruption, loss, misuse, or irreversible mistakes. It adds safeguards, reversibility, monitoring, and repair paths before users encounter the breakdown.

This level goes beyond implementing requested features. Designers actively explore harmful interactions and remain available to correct problems discovered after delivery.

14094.title: Descriptor Matching
14094.heading: Descriptor Matching
14094.content:
Descriptor matching compares feature descriptors to propose which observed image points correspond to known model points. Similarity or distance in descriptor space supplies candidates, often with a test that rejects matches that are not sufficiently distinctive.

Appearance similarity can still produce false pairs in repeated or ambiguous texture. A robust geometric estimator tests whether a subset of matches agrees with one camera pose and discards inconsistent outliers.

14097.title: Descriptive Analysis
14097.heading: Descriptive Analysis
14097.content:
Descriptive analysis characterizes the observations in an [[Analytic Dataset]] before multivariable modeling. It summarizes distributions, reports the prevalence or average of outcomes, and examines how exposures and candidate confounders vary across relevant groups.

Its main deliverables combine tables, graphs, and bivariate tests. Description is not merely preliminary decoration: it can reveal implausible codes, sparse cells, missingness, skewness, or confounding patterns that change how the later model should be specified.

14118.title: Derivative
14118.heading: Derivative
14118.content:
A derivative describes the rate at which a function changes at a particular point. Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line at that point.

Its sign provides local directional information. If increasing a parameter produces a negative derivative of loss, the loss decreases; if the derivative is positive, increasing that parameter raises the loss. A multivariable function has a [[Partial Derivative]] for each variable.

Formally, the derivative is the limit of the difference quotient $(f(x+h)-f(x))/h$ as $h$ approaches zero, when that limit exists. Higher derivatives describe changes in earlier derivatives, and the second derivative supplies curvature information for identifying local extrema.

14120.sourceSearchName: derivative of exponential function derivative of exponential function

14121.sourceSearchName: derivative of exponential function derivative of exponential function
14121.title: Derivative of Exponential Function
14121.heading: Derivative of Exponential Function
14121.content:
The natural exponential function is characterized by

$$\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.$$

More generally, $d(a^x)/dx=a^x\ln a$ for $a>0$. When the exponent is itself a function, the [[Chain Rule]] gives $d(e^{g(x)})/dx=e^{g(x)}g'(x)$.

14122.title: Derivative of Exponential Function
14122.heading: References

14124.title: Derivative Function
14124.heading: Derivative Function
14124.content:
The derivative function assigns to each differentiable input $x$ the limit

$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$

It records the original function's instantaneous rate of change across its domain. Its sign describes local increase or decrease, and differentiating it again produces higher-order change.

14127.sourceSearchName: derivative of logarithmic function derivative of logarithmic function
14127.title: Derivative of Logarithmic Function
14127.heading: Derivative of Logarithmic Function
14127.content:
For $x>0$, the natural logarithm satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac{1}{x}.$$

This follows from the inverse relationship between logarithm and exponential functions. With a differentiable inner function, the [[Chain Rule]] gives $d(\ln g(x))/dx=g'(x)/g(x)$ wherever $g(x)>0$.

14130.title: Derivation
14130.heading: Derivation
14130.content:
A derivation is a sequence of [[Production Rule|production-rule]] applications that begins with a grammar's start symbol and produces another string. A terminal-only result belongs to the language generated by the grammar.

A left derivation always replaces the leftmost nonterminal, while a right derivation always replaces the rightmost. Restricting the order removes irrelevant differences and makes ambiguity and parsing procedures easier to analyze through a [[Parse Tree]].

14133.title: Depth of Field
14133.heading: Depth of Field
14133.content:
Depth of field is the range of scene distances that appear acceptably focused. It changes with aperture, focal length, focus distance, and acceptable blur: a smaller aperture generally extends the focused range, while a wider aperture makes it shallower.

Because depth-dependent blur should vary coherently across a real scene, it can test both exposure metadata and a composite's geometry. Inserted objects whose sharpness does not fit their apparent distance may violate the camera model that explains the rest of the photograph.

14142.title: Depth Lemma
14142.heading: Depth Lemma
14142.content:
The depth lemma relates depths in a [[Short Exact Sequence]] 0 → M₁ → M₂ → M₃ → 0. Each module's depth is bounded below by a minimum formed from the other two, with a one-degree shift where appropriate.

These inequalities arise from the [[Long Exact Sequence in Ext]]. They let depth information propagate through submodules, extensions, and quotients without constructing regular sequences directly.

14145.title: Depth Cue
14145.heading: Depth Cue
14145.content:
A depth cue is information the visual system uses to infer the spatial structure and distance of objects. Depth cues support [[Object Selection]], [[3D Manipulation]], and [[Navigation]].

Static monocular cues include relative size, height relative to the horizon, occlusion, linear and aerial perspective, shadows, lighting, and texture gradients. Motion can provide parallax. The eyes also supply cues through [[Accommodation]], [[Vergence]], and binocular disparity.

Cues can reinforce or contradict one another. A display that presents inconsistent depth information can cause false spatial judgments, discomfort, or reduced performance, so cue support is an important part of [[Display Fidelity]].

14148.title: Deployment Stage
14148.heading: Deployment Stage
14148.content:
A deployment stage applies a selected build artifact and environment configuration to a target. Stages let a release pipeline model destinations such as staging and production as ordered steps with separate variables and conditions.

The stage should deploy an existing artifact rather than silently compile a new one. This preserves the evidence gathered earlier in the pipeline as the release advances.

14151.content: The dependency inversion principle directs high-level behavior to depend on abstractions rather than concrete details. An inventory command can require an `IInventoryReadContext` contract instead of constructing a particular database or in-memory repository. [[Dependency Injection]] is one way to provide the implementation, but the principle concerns the dependency direction itself: changing storage should not require rewriting the command's business rule.

14154.title: Deployment Environment
14154.heading: Deployment Environment
14154.content:
A deployment environment is a named operating context with its own configuration, infrastructure, diagnostics, and security expectations. Development, staging, and production environments let the same application select settings appropriate to different parts of delivery.

ASP.NET Core can load environment-specific configuration files and behavior. The environment name should be set by the host rather than embedded into the application source.

14160.title: Dependency Graph
14160.heading: Dependency Graph
14160.content:
A dependency graph records which values or objects must be updated when another value changes. Unlike a scene graph's spatial hierarchy, its edges express computation: a tracked pose may affect a transformation, which affects a camera, which affects a rendered image.

Combining dependency and scene relationships lets an AR framework update derived state without hard-coding one procedural sequence. The scheduler still must handle cycles and timing constraints deliberately.

14163.title: Dependency Injection
14163.heading: Dependency Injection
14163.content:
Dependency injection supplies an object with its collaborators instead of making it construct or locate them itself. This reduces hard-coded dependencies and supports reuse, readability, configuration, and isolated testing.

ASP.NET Core registers application services during startup and injects them into consumers such as controllers. Angular applies the same design principle to components and services, allowing an [[Angular HttpClient]] or a custom [[Data Service]] to be supplied through a constructor.

In the inventory application, commands depend on read or write context interfaces and the .NET service provider supplies their implementations through constructor injection. Registration also specifies whether an instance is transient, scoped, or shared as a singleton; this construction policy is distinct from the business behavior of the command.

14166.title: DenStream
14166.heading: DenStream
14166.content:
DenStream maintains fading microclusters for evolving data and applies a density-based offline procedure to their current summaries. Potential core microclusters represent stable dense regions, while outlier microclusters track sparse candidates that may grow or disappear.

Exponential decay reduces the influence of old observations and enables adaptation to concept drift. Decay rate and density thresholds determine how quickly genuine new clusters emerge and how long inactive structure persists.

14169.title: Density-Reachable Cluster
14169.heading: Density-Reachable Cluster
14169.content:
Density reachability defines a cluster through chains of sufficiently populated neighborhoods. A core observation has enough neighbors within a fixed radius, and another observation is density-reachable when a sequence of core-mediated steps connects them.

This relation allows dense regions of arbitrary shape to become clusters while isolated observations remain noise. A single radius and minimum-neighbor threshold can struggle when different parts of the dataset have substantially different densities.

A density-based outlier lies in a region substantially sparser than the relevant surrounding data. It is judged relative to local concentration rather than one global distance threshold.

This perspective handles variable-density data better than a simple radius rule, but estimating neighborhood density and selecting its scale can be computationally demanding.

This generalizes a point-based local density estimate to uncertain observations. The kernel scale and uncertainty model jointly determine which training cases influence the decision, so excessive smoothing can erase real class boundaries.

14184.title: Dense Layer
14184.heading: Dense Layer
14184.content:
A dense layer is a [[Neural Network Layer]] in which every neuron receives connections from every unit in the preceding layer. Each connection has its own [[Neural Network Weight]], and each receiving neuron has a bias.

Dense connectivity is simple and flexible but creates many parameters. A layer of 128 neurons following 784 input values requires 100,352 separate connection weights, illustrating how network size can grow even with only a few layers.

14187.title: Denominator
14187.heading: Denominator
14187.content:
The denominator is the lower, nonzero component (n) of a [[Fraction]] (m/n). It specifies the number of equal parts into which a unit is divided and serves as the divisor in (m\div n).

The condition (n\neq0) is essential because division by zero is undefined. Fractions with different denominators can be compared, added, or subtracted by converting them to a [[Common Denominator]]. Increasing the denominator while preserving the same numerator generally makes each represented part smaller.

14190.title: Denoising Autoencoder
14190.heading: Denoising Autoencoder
14190.content:
A denoising autoencoder receives a corrupted version of an input but is trained to reconstruct the clean original. Successful reconstruction requires learning stable structure rather than simply copying individual values.

The corruption process defines which variations the representation should ignore. Features learned this way can be more robust and can initialize deeper models or support downstream tasks.

14193.title: Dendrogram
14193.heading: Dendrogram
14193.content:
A dendrogram is a tree diagram for a hierarchical clustering. Each node represents a cluster, connecting lines show which groups are nested, and the vertical level records when a merge or split occurs.

A horizontal cut through the dendrogram selects one partition from the hierarchy. The diagram makes the sequence visible, but the chosen cut still requires a stopping rule and substantive interpretation.

In the source's tissue example, leaf colors reveal whether an unsupervised hierarchy corresponds to known biological groups. Changes caused by feature scaling or by replacing all genes with leading principal components demonstrate that the tree depends on the representation and distance used.

Murtagh treats a ranked dendrogram as an ultrametric representation: the level of the first common ancestor gives a tree-derived distance between two leaves. Reversing the left and right children at a node changes the drawing order but preserves nested membership. A root-to-leaf path can also carry signed details in a hierarchical Haar transform, turning the tree into a multiscale data encoding.

Capacity planning, distribution, graceful degradation, rate controls, failover, and recovery can limit the outcome. Detection still matters, but continued function and restoration are the decisive measures.

14199.title: DENCLUE
14199.heading: DENCLUE
14199.content:
DENCLUE models overall data density as the sum of influence functions centered on individual observations. Clusters are associated with density attractors reached by following the gradient of that estimated density, subject to a minimum-density condition.

The formulation provides a mathematical connection between density estimation and clustering and can handle irregular shapes and noise. Bandwidth and density thresholds control which modes survive and whether nearby high-density regions are joined.

14202.title: Demosaicing
14202.heading: Demosaicing
14202.content:
Demosaicing reconstructs a full red-green-blue image from the single-channel samples recorded through a [[Color Filter Array]]. For each location, the camera retains the measured channel and estimates the two missing channels from nearby values according to its interpolation algorithm.

This process means that roughly two-thirds of displayed color values are computed rather than directly sensed. The resulting periodic relationships can identify a camera-processing pipeline and can be disrupted when an editor replaces or transforms a region.

14211.title: Degrees of Freedom
14211.heading: Degrees of Freedom
14211.content:
Degrees of freedom are the independent dimensions in which a body can move. They describe the possible motion of an [[Input Device]], an articulated body part, or a virtual object.

A tracker commonly reports six degrees of freedom: translation along the x, y, and z axes and rotation as yaw, pitch, and roll. The number of degrees a device can sense indicates some of its capacity, but control integration also matters. Six values controlled together by one coordinated movement behave differently from values split across several controls.

Reducing unnecessary degrees of freedom can make [[3D Manipulation]] or [[3D Travel]] more precise and easier to control.

14226.heading: Defining Scene Orientation from Tracking Data
14226.content:
A successful camera solve may still be rotated strangely relative to Blender's world axes. The Orientation controls use tracked references to define which direction and plane should act as the floor or a wall.

Defining a plane requires three solved markers with bundles that cover the solver's key frames. Trying another suitable set can improve alignment when reference geometry fails to match the physical surfaces visible in the footage.

The broader matchmove workflow in Gress's book likewise treats scene origin and orientation as necessary steps after a camera path and point cloud have been calculated. A test object should remain locked to the physical scene before a finished CG element is placed. See [[3D Camera Solve from Feature Tracks]].

14229.title: Deferred Shading
14229.heading: Deferred Shading
14229.content:
Deferred shading separates surface rendering from lighting. The first pass writes visible surface properties into a [[G-Buffer]], and a later pass reads those screen-space values to evaluate global and local lights.

The approach avoids repeating complex geometry work for every light and performs well with many lights. It consumes substantial render-target memory and complicates transparency, which is commonly handled later with forward rendering.

14232.heading: Deferred Actor Removal
14232.content:
Deferred actor removal marks an actor for deletion during an update but erases it only after the active actor iteration finishes. This prevents iterator invalidation and use-after-free errors when an actor destroys itself or another actor mid-frame.

New actors may likewise be collected in a pending list until the current traversal completes. The world then applies additions and removals at a controlled synchronization point.

Defense in depth protects a system with multiple security layers so that the failure of one control does not expose the entire environment. The source applies this idea across the [[Human Security Layer]], [[Network Security Layer]], [[Host Security Layer]], [[Application Security Layer]], and [[Data Security States]], with cloud and mobile systems crossing several layers.

The layers should reinforce one another. Prevention reduces opportunities for attack, detection reveals activity that crosses a boundary, and response limits the consequences when an attack succeeds.

14246.title: Deep Boltzmann Machine
14246.heading: Document

14247.sourceSearchName: deep boltzmann machine deep boltzmann machine
14247.title: Deep Boltzmann Machine
14247.heading: Deep Boltzmann Machine
14247.content:
A deep Boltzmann machine is an undirected graphical model with multiple layers of hidden variables. Interactions across layers let it represent complex dependencies and learn hierarchical latent features.

Unlike a directed stack, inference involves jointly explaining observations through the hidden layers. This expressiveness makes both inference and training computationally demanding and dependent on approximation.

14249.title: Deep Neural Network
14249.heading: Document

14250.sourceSearchName: deep neural network deep neural network
14250.title: Deep Neural Network
14250.heading: Deep Neural Network
14250.content:
A deep neural network is an [[Artificial Neural Network]] with multiple learned layers between input and output. Successive layers can transform raw features into progressively more useful internal representations.

Depth lets a system learn complex mappings used in speech and language, but it also increases demands for data, computation, and careful optimization through [[Backpropagation]].

Each [[Hidden Layer]] encodes a transformation of the representation produced before it. Successive layers can therefore build a hierarchy of concepts: an image network might progress from local edges to parts and then complete objects. This increasing level of abstraction is the sense in which the network and its learning are described as deep.

Kelleher counts [[Neural Depth Counting|depth]] by learned transformations: the hidden layers plus the output layer, or the number of weight matrices crossed. The input layer merely presents values. Additional depth increases representational flexibility, but it can also aggravate the [[Vanishing Gradient Problem]] unless the architecture and training setup support useful backward signals.

14251.sourceSearchName: deep neural network deep neural network
14251.title: Deep Neural Network
14251.heading: References

14253.title: Deep Learning
14253.heading: Deep Learning
14253.content:
Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks to learn increasingly abstract representations from data. The method can model complex relationships without requiring every useful feature to be specified manually.

Its usefulness in automated business analytics depends on adequate data, computation, evaluation, and a clear connection to the target decision. Model depth does not remove the need to test results outside the data used for fitting.

14255.sourceSearchName: deep belief network deep belief network
14255.title: Deep Belief Network
14255.heading: Document

14256.sourceSearchName: deep belief network deep belief network
14256.title: Deep Belief Network
14256.heading: Deep Belief Network
14256.content:
A deep belief network stacks latent layers so that higher levels capture progressively abstract structure. It can be initialized by training restricted Boltzmann machines one layer at a time and then refined for a generative or supervised task.

Layer-wise learning historically made deep representation training more feasible. The final hidden activations can serve as derived features even when the network is later paired with a separate predictor.

14259.title: Decorator Pattern
14259.heading: Decorator Pattern
14259.content: A decorator implements the same interface as an object it wraps, delegates the core operation to that object, and adds behavior around it. The book's message decorators change console color while leaving simple or alert message classes responsible for their own output. Wrapping can be composed or selected at runtime, extending behavior without requiring a subclass for every combination of features.

14262.title: Decoupled Simulation
14262.heading: Decoupled Simulation
14262.content:
Decoupled simulation separates application or world-state computation from the tracking and display processes that observe and render it. Each part can update at an appropriate rate and communicate through defined state or event interfaces.

The separation supports distribution, testing, and replacement of components, but it introduces synchronization work. The renderer must use a coherent simulation state and current pose rather than combining values from incompatible times.

14264.sourceSearchName: decision oriented design meeting decision oriented design meeting
14264.title: Decision-Oriented Design Meeting
14264.heading: Document

14265.sourceSearchName: decision oriented design meeting decision oriented design meeting
14265.title: Decision-Oriented Design Meeting
14265.heading: Decision-Oriented Design Meeting
14265.content:
A decision-oriented design meeting has a defined purpose, prepared questions, appropriate participants, and an explicit record of conclusions and actions. It uses synchronous time for issues that need interaction rather than for reporting information that could be shared asynchronously.

Closing the meeting requires identifying what was decided, what remains open, who will act, and when the result will be reviewed. Without that conversion, discussion creates motion but not progress.

14266.sourceSearchName: decision oriented design meeting decision oriented design meeting
14266.title: Decision-Oriented Design Meeting
14266.heading: References

14268.title: Decision-Making
14268.heading: Decision-Making
14268.content:
Decision-making is the process of choosing between alternatives with real or imagined consequences. It depends on recognizing the current situation, identifying possible actions, and considering their outcomes.

Its speed is affected by conflict, complexity, and uncertainty. Normative models emphasize rational choice, behavioral models account for human limitations and heuristics, and naturalistic models examine decisions made during realistic complex tasks.

In [[Information Processing]], decision-making connects perception and knowledge to action. [[Situation Awareness]] supplies an internal model of the environment, while learned behavior and [[Skill Acquisition|skills]] can make common responses faster and more accurate.

In games, a [[Meaningful Decision]] changes discernible state, future possibilities, or progress toward a goal. Uncertainty makes prediction relevant, while a dominant strategy or equivalent alternatives collapse the decision space into an apparent choice with no practical consequence.

14271.title: Decision-Making as a Design Value
14271.heading: Decision-Making as a Design Value
14271.content:
A decision-making design value specifies where players should choose, which consequences should matter, and how much information should be available at the moment of choice. It identifies the intended relationship between deliberation and action.

This value can call for transparent optimization, bluffing under hidden information, rapid commitment, or reflective ambiguity. The interface and feedback should preserve that intended decision condition rather than accidentally resolving or obscuring it.

14273.sourceSearchName: decision level multimedia fusion decision level multimedia fusion
14273.title: Decision-Level Multimedia Fusion
14273.heading: Document

14274.sourceSearchName: decision level multimedia fusion decision level multimedia fusion
14274.title: Decision-Level Multimedia Fusion
14274.heading: Decision-Level Multimedia Fusion
14274.content:
Decision-level multimedia fusion trains separate classifiers for different modalities and combines their predicted labels or probabilities. Each model can use features and algorithms suited to its own signal.

Late fusion is robust when a channel is missing and permits modality-specific calibration, but it cannot learn low-level interactions discarded before combination. Voting, weighted scores, or a learned combiner determine the final class.

14275.sourceSearchName: decision level multimedia fusion decision level multimedia fusion
14275.title: Decision-Level Multimedia Fusion
14275.heading: References

14277.title: Decision Visualization
14277.heading: Decision Visualization
14277.content:
Decision visualization presents data and analytical results in forms that help people compare alternatives, detect patterns, and understand consequences. Its purpose is not only to display output but to incorporate evidence into the reasoning process.

A useful visual representation matches the decision, exposes uncertainty and scale, and avoids hiding important variation through aggregation. The display mediates between an analytical pipeline and human judgment.

14280.title: Decision Variable
14280.heading: Decision Variable
14280.content:
A decision variable represents a quantity whose value the optimization process is allowed to choose. Examples include production amounts, resource allocations, or activity levels.

Its coefficients in the [[Linear Objective Function]] measure value or cost, while its coefficients in each [[Linear Constraint]] measure resource use or other effects.

14283.title: Decision Tree
14283.heading: Decision Tree
14283.content:
A decision tree represents classification as a hierarchy of attribute tests. Internal nodes test features, branches correspond to outcomes, and leaf nodes return class labels.

Every root-to-leaf path can be read as an if-then rule. Tree depth and branching affect storage, search cost, and interpretability.

The book fits a classification tree as an interpretable baseline, examines its splits and variable importance, and applies it to held-out data. The contrast between training and validation results shows why readable structure does not eliminate the need for independent evaluation.

14285.sourceSearchName: decision tree overfitting decision tree overfitting
14285.title: Decision Tree Overfitting
14285.heading: Document

14286.sourceSearchName: decision tree overfitting decision tree overfitting
14286.title: Decision Tree Overfitting
14286.heading: Decision Tree Overfitting
14286.content:
Decision tree overfitting occurs when branches reproduce noise or accidental details of the training sample rather than a stable classification relationship. It is encouraged by small, unrepresentative, or noisy data sets.

An overfit tree can classify its training examples perfectly while performing poorly on new cases. Early stopping, pruning, validation data, statistical tests, or complexity penalties can reduce the problem.

The book demonstrates overfitting when a tree or ensemble performs exceptionally on training records but worse on validation data. Complexity and loss settings are tuned against held-out performance rather than the apparent perfection of the fitted sample.

14287.sourceSearchName: decision tree overfitting decision tree overfitting
14287.title: Decision Tree Overfitting
14287.heading: References

14288.sourceSearchName: decision tree attribute selection decision tree attribute selection
14288.title: Decision Tree Attribute Selection
14288.heading: Document

14289.sourceSearchName: decision tree attribute selection decision tree attribute selection
14289.title: Decision Tree Attribute Selection
14289.heading: Decision Tree Attribute Selection
14289.content:
Decision tree attribute selection chooses the feature used to split the examples at a non-leaf node. Entropy-based methods compare the expected class uncertainty remaining after each candidate split.

The choice shapes every lower branch. An attribute used as a split is removed from later consideration in the basic ID3 procedure because repeating it adds no new information.

14290.sourceSearchName: decision tree attribute selection decision tree attribute selection
14290.title: Decision Tree Attribute Selection
14290.heading: References

14291.sourceSearchName: decision rule path decision rule path
14291.title: Decision Rule Path
14291.heading: Document

14292.sourceSearchName: decision rule path decision rule path
14292.title: Decision Rule Path
14292.heading: Decision Rule Path
14292.content:
A decision rule path is the conjunction of attribute-value tests encountered from a decision tree's root to one leaf. The leaf label supplies the consequence of the corresponding if-then rule.

Extracting one rule per path turns a tree into an explicit rule set. Pruning can remove conditions that mainly reflect noise.

14293.sourceSearchName: decision rule path decision rule path
14293.title: Decision Rule Path
14293.heading: References

14295.title: Decision Boundary
14295.heading: Decision Boundary
14295.content:
A decision boundary separates the regions of input space that a [[Classifier]] assigns to different outcomes. In two dimensions it can be visualized as a line or curve between classes.

A single [[Perceptron]] can learn only a linear boundary, so it handles data that can be divided by one straight line. An [[Artificial Neural Network]] with hidden layers can combine neuron outputs to represent more complicated, nonlinear boundaries.

Kelleher's two-input threshold-neuron example makes the geometry concrete. The boundary is perpendicular to the neuron's input-weight vector; altering the weights rotates it, while a [[Neural Network Bias|bias term]] moves it off the origin. That separates the effects of weight direction and threshold position on which [[Model Input Space|input points]] receive high activation.

14298.title: Decider
14298.heading: Decider
14298.content:
A decider is a logical branch that routes a flow according to internal state, available resources, or external conditions. It represents a decision point inside a system model.

The conditions governing a decider should remain near the same organizational level and operational context as the decision. Excessive dependence across distant levels makes a [[System]] harder to understand and more brittle.

14301.title: Decibel Scale
14301.heading: Decibel Scale
14301.content:
The decibel scale expresses an intensity ratio logarithmically:

$$L=10\log_{10}(I/I_0)\ \mathrm{dB}.$$

For sound, $I_0$ is commonly the threshold reference intensity. A tenfold intensity increase adds 10 dB, while doubling intensity adds about 3 dB. Decibels compare levels rather than serving as an absolute SI unit.

14304.title: Decarbonized Biomanufacturing
14304.heading: Decarbonized Biomanufacturing
14304.content:
Decarbonized biomanufacturing powers cell-based production with low-emission energy and reduces carbon-intensive inputs and logistics. This matters because cultured products replace biological methane or land burdens partly with facility electricity.

Environmental forecasts cannot treat today's grid as permanent; cleaner energy can improve future results, while fossil-heavy electricity can erase expected advantages.

14307.title: DEC PDP-8
14307.heading: DEC PDP-8
14307.content:
The PDP-8 was a compact, relatively inexpensive 12-bit minicomputer introduced in 1965. Standard transistor modules and automated wire-wrap construction reduced its size and cost.

DEC shared design information so customers could embed the machine in laboratories, factories, telephone systems, and medical instruments. This openness made general-purpose computing adaptable to specialized work.

14310.title: DEC PDP-1
14310.heading: DEC PDP-1
14310.content:
The PDP-1 was Digital Equipment Corporation’s first computer, introduced in 1960 as a programmed data processor. Its transistorized design supported direct interactive use outside the traditional batch-oriented computer room.

Researchers used it for graphics, music, games, and experimental interfaces. The machine helped establish a culture of hands-on computing that fed later networking and personal systems.

14313.title: Debugger
14313.heading: Debugger
14313.content:
A debugger runs a program under controlled conditions so a developer can inspect its behavior and changing state. It can pause execution, step through instructions, and display variables, the call stack, and other runtime information.

In a full-stack application, [[Server-Side Debugging]] follows .NET request handling while [[Client-Side Debugging]] follows TypeScript and browser behavior. Both use breakpoints to stop at relevant operations.

14316.title: Debug and Trace in .NET
14316.heading: Debug and Trace in .NET
14316.content:
The .NET `Debug` and `Trace` facilities emit diagnostic messages without coupling application logic to direct console output. Debug instrumentation is associated with development builds, while trace output can be compiled for release and observed during runtime.

Conditional compilation controls whether calls participate in a build, and listeners determine where emitted events go. This separates the decision to record an event from the destination that stores or displays it.

14319.title: Deadlock Avoidance
14319.heading: Deadlock Avoidance
14319.content:
A deadlock arises when participants wait permanently for resources held by one another. A classic case occurs when two threads acquire the same pair of locks in opposite orders and each waits for the lock held by the other.

Consistent lock ordering, smaller critical sections, time-bounded acquisition, and fewer shared resources reduce the risk. Asynchronous code should also avoid synchronously blocking on incomplete tasks, which can create a waiting cycle with a captured execution context.

14322.heading: Deadline-Aware MapReduce Scheduling
14322.content:
Deadline-aware MapReduce scheduling estimates the map and reduce capacity a job needs to finish by a specified time. It can treat completion as a constraint while minimizing resources, cost, or the number of missed deadlines.

Reliable estimates must account for input size, task duration, data placement, cluster heterogeneity, phase dependencies, and contention from other jobs.

14325.title: Dead-End Reward
14325.heading: Dead-End Reward
14325.content:
A dead-end reward acknowledges or entices the player without feeding back into the main game system. A noninteractive story segment or platform-level [[Achievement]] may be rewarding while leaving the player's available verbs, resources, and choices unchanged.

These rewards can still provide rest, meaning, or motivation, but they risk eclipsing the pleasure of play when the player treats gameplay only as a barrier to the next payoff.

14328.title: de Broglie Wavelength
14328.heading: de Broglie Wavelength
14328.content:
The de Broglie relation assigns wavelength to a particle with momentum $p$:

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}.$$

For a nonrelativistic particle, $p=mv$. Greater momentum produces shorter wavelength, so wave effects are readily observed for microscopic particles but become negligibly small for everyday objects.

14331.sourceSearchName: dct coefficient histogram dct coefficient histogram
14331.title: DCT Coefficient Histogram
14331.heading: DCT Coefficient Histogram
14331.content:
A DCT coefficient histogram counts how often a selected discrete-cosine-transform coefficient takes each value across JPEG blocks. Ordinary single compression usually produces a comparatively smooth distribution centered around zero, with shape varying by spatial frequency and image content.

Periodic holes and peaks can expose [[Double Quantization Artifact]]. Analysts examine several frequencies because not every coefficient carries a clear trace, and heavy recompression or limited image area can weaken the statistical evidence.

14334.title: DbUp
14334.heading: DbUp
14334.content:
DbUp is a .NET library for applying ordered database change scripts. It records which scripts have run, discovers pending scripts, and executes them so the database schema advances with the application.

The book configures migrations during application startup and packages SQL as embedded resources. A production workflow should still control when and under which identity those schema-changing operations execute.
